# 2D: AI

## Guide
- [Enemy patrol and chase](./Enemy-Patrol-and-Chase.md)

## Common patterns
Waypoint patrols provide predictable movement; distance tests detect nearby targets; Physics2D raycasts can check line of sight. Add explicit states as behavior grows: Patrol, Chase, Attack, Return, and Stunned are common examples.

## Debugging
Draw the detection ray, show waypoint gizmos, validate layer masks, and ensure AI does not compete with another controller for the same Rigidbody2D. Distance-only detection sees through walls unless you test occlusion.

# 2D: Animation

## Guides
- [Sprite animation and Animator](./Sprite-Animation-and-Animator.md)
- [Sprite flipping and aiming](./Sprite-Flipping-and-Aiming.md)

## Workflow
Import the sheet as Sprite (2D and UI), slice sprites in Sprite Editor, and create animation clips. Use an Animator Controller when states/parameters/transitions are useful; direct sprite assignment may suffice for very simple animations.

## Animator checks
Animator references the correct controller, clips are present in states, transition conditions refer to existing parameters with matching types, looping clips have Loop Time enabled, and no two systems control the same Transform property.

## Sprite consistency
Keep Pixels Per Unit and pivots consistent between frames. Use SpriteRenderer sorting/layers independently of physics layers. Test flipping with child weapons/colliders so visuals and hitboxes remain aligned.

# 2D: Audio

## Guide
- [Audio setup and sound effects](./Audio-Setup-and-Sound-Effects.md)

## AudioSource basics
- AudioClip: imported audio asset.
- AudioSource: playback component.
- AudioListener: usually on the active camera; keep a single active listener.
- AudioMixer: groups sources and controls volume/effects centrally.

For positional 2D effects, Spatial Blend is normally 0. Disable Play On Awake for code-triggered effects. Use PlayOneShot for short overlapping sounds; use looping AudioSources for music/ambience as appropriate.

## Import and performance
Audio import settings trade memory, latency, and CPU use. Choose based on clip duration and target platform. Profile rather than selecting one setting for every sound.

## Troubleshooting
Check source/listener enabled states, assigned clips, source volume, mixer routing/mute, Spatial Blend, pause state, and platform audio settings.

# 2D: Cameras

## Guides
- [Camera follow and pixel-perfect setup](./Camera-Follow-and-Pixel-Perfect.md)
- [Camera bounds and level confinement](./Camera-Bounds.md)
- [Screen shake recipe](../Recipes/Screen-Shake.md)

## Orthographic projection
Orthographic Size is half of the visible vertical world span. Visible width depends on aspect ratio. Set a deliberate camera Z position and ensure the gameplay plane is in front of the camera.

## Follow and confinement
Use LateUpdate for many simple follow cameras, or a camera package such as Cinemachine for richer rigs. Bounds must account for the camera's half-width and half-height. Integrate smoothing and clamping so one does not undo the other.

## Pixel art
Keep PPU/reference resolution consistent and test actual target resolution. Fractional camera positions can create shimmer or uneven pixel movement.

docs.content:
# 2D Component Inspector Reference

Property names can change between Unity releases. This guide explains the purpose of common settings; use the installed Editor's tooltip and version-specific documentation for exact labels.

## SpriteRenderer

| Property | Purpose / when to change it |
|---|---|
| Sprite | Image asset drawn by this renderer. |
| Color | Tints the sprite; alpha can make it transparent. |
| Flip X / Flip Y | Mirrors the rendered sprite without rotating the GameObject. |
| Draw Mode | Simple, Sliced, or Tiled behaviour where supported. |
| Sorting Layer | Broad draw-order category. |
| Order in Layer | Relative draw order inside the sorting layer. |
| Mask Interaction | Controls interaction with Sprite Masks. |
| Material | Shader/material used to render the sprite. |

## Rigidbody2D

| Property | Purpose / caution |
|---|---|
| Body Type | Dynamic, Kinematic, or Static simulation behaviour. |
| Simulated | Whether the body participates in 2D physics. |
| Mass | Affects force response; changing mass does not necessarily change gravity acceleration. |
| Gravity Scale | Multiplies gravity for this body. |
| Linear / Angular Damping | Reduces linear/angular motion over time; labels vary by Unity version. |
| Collision Detection | Discrete is cheaper; Continuous may help fast bodies avoid tunnelling. |
| Interpolate | Smooths rendered movement between physics updates. |
| Constraints | Freeze position or rotation axes when appropriate. |

## Collider2D

| Property | Purpose / caution |
|---|---|
| Is Trigger | Reports overlap events instead of ordinary solid collision response. |
| Material | Physics Material 2D for friction/bounciness. |
| Offset | Moves the collider relative to its object. |
| Size / Radius / Points | Defines collision geometry, depending on shape. |
| Used by Composite | Lets compatible colliders contribute to a Composite Collider 2D. |

## Animator

- **Controller:** state machine asset to evaluate.
- **Avatar:** rig mapping where applicable.
- **Apply Root Motion:** applies animation-authored displacement; coordinate this with scripted movement.
- **Update Mode:** controls evaluation timing.
- **Culling Mode:** determines whether animation is evaluated when not visible.

## Diagnostic order
1. Confirm component enabled and GameObject active.
2. Confirm all serialized references are assigned.
3. Confirm layer and sorting configuration.
4. Confirm physics body type and collider dimensions.
5. Check Console errors and package/version mismatch.
6. Reproduce in a minimal test scene before changing many settings.

Official references: [SpriteRenderer](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/SpriteRenderer.html) · [Rigidbody2D](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Rigidbody2D.html) · [Collider2D](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Collider2D.html)

docs.title: 2D: Components
docs.content:
# 2D: Components

## Common components
- **SpriteRenderer:** draws a sprite. Important fields include Sprite, Color, Flip X/Y, Draw Mode, Mask Interaction, Sorting Layer, and Order in Layer.
- **Rigidbody2D:** controls 2D simulation. Review Body Type, Simulated, Mass, Gravity Scale, Linear/Angular Damping (names vary by version), Collision Detection, Interpolate, and Constraints.
- **Collider2D:** defines a collision shape. Common types: Box, Circle, Capsule, Polygon, Edge, Composite.
- **Animator:** evaluates an Animator Controller and its parameters to select visual states.
- **SortingGroup:** sorts a group of renderers together, useful for multi-sprite characters.

Detailed settings reference: [2D Component Inspector Reference](./Inspector-Reference.md).

## Choosing components
Use the simplest collider that supports the gameplay. Add Rigidbody2D when an object needs physics simulation or relevant collision/trigger interactions. Static level geometry generally does not need to be moved by script.

## Inspector checklist
1. Are references assigned?
2. Is the Rigidbody2D Body Type appropriate?
3. Are colliders enabled and sized correctly?
4. Is Is Trigger set as intended?
5. Do the involved layers interact in the Physics 2D Layer Collision Matrix?
6. Are sorting layer and order correct?

## Common mistakes
A collider alone does not make an object move. Directly changing Transform on a physics body can produce unreliable contacts. A trigger callback can fail due to missing Rigidbody2D setup, disabled objects, or layer filtering.

Official reference: [2D physics components](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/Physics2DReference.html)

docs.title: 2D Coordinate Spaces and Pixels Per Unit
docs.content:
# 2D Coordinate Spaces and Pixels Per Unit

## World space and screen space
World coordinates describe the game scene. Screen coordinates describe pixel positions in the game window. UI coordinates may use a Canvas-specific space. Convert between them explicitly.

```csharp
Vector3 screen = Input.mousePosition;
Vector3 world = Camera.main.ScreenToWorldPoint(
    new Vector3(screen.x, screen.y, -Camera.main.transform.position.z));
```

This example assumes a 2D scene on the XY plane with a camera looking along Z. For production code, cache a camera reference instead of repeatedly using Camera.main, and account for the camera's orientation and desired depth.

## Pixels Per Unit (PPU)
PPU specifies how many source-image pixels represent one world unit. For example, a 32-pixel-wide sprite imported at 32 PPU is approximately one world unit wide before Transform scaling.

Consistency matters more than a particular PPU number. If some assets use 16 PPU and others use 100 PPU, they may appear at very different sizes unless their import settings and Transform scales are planned.

## Pixels and filtering
- **Point:** preserves crisp pixel boundaries, often preferred for pixel art.
- **Bilinear:** smooths texture sampling.
- **Compression:** may reduce memory but can introduce artifacts.
- **Mip Maps:** commonly useful for textures viewed at varying scales; evaluate their suitability for 2D UI and pixel art.

## Camera sizing
An orthographic camera's Size is half the vertical view span in world units. Horizontal span depends on the aspect ratio. Test several window shapes, especially if the game uses a fixed pixel-art resolution.

## Pixel-perfect checklist
1. Consistent PPU across the art set.
2. Point filtering when appropriate.
3. Deliberate reference resolution.
4. Camera movement aligned with the chosen pixel grid if required.
5. Test at target resolutions and aspect ratios.

Reference: [Sprite import settings](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/texture-type-sprite.html)

docs.content:
# Unity Localization and Accessibility Setup

Unity's Localization package supports translated strings, locale-specific assets, Smart Strings for values/plurals, pseudo-localization, and import/export workflows. Package availability and APIs depend on the installed Unity version.

Official Unity 6 manual: https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/com.unity.localization.html

## Install and create tables
1. Install the Localization package through Package Manager.
2. Open the Localization Settings workflow and create a Localization Settings asset if prompted.
3. Add the locales your game needs (for example, English and another target language).
4. Create a String Table Collection such as UI.
5. Give entries stable keys such as menu.play, menu.settings, and game.pause.
6. Enter translations per locale instead of hardcoding visible sentences throughout scripts.
7. Add a Localize String Event or LocalizedString binding to UI elements supported by the chosen UI system.
8. For language selection, set the selected locale through the package's documented API and save the user's preference.

Exact menu locations and UI components can vary by package version. Follow the documentation for your installed package.

## Localized assets
The package can provide different assets for different locales. This is useful when art contains text, audio is dubbed, or a region requires a different graphic. Avoid embedding text inside images if it could instead be translated as text.

## Text layout
Translations may be much longer or shorter than the source. Test buttons, subtitles, dialogs, text wrapping, font glyph coverage, and right-to-left layouts if supported. Avoid hardcoded widths that only fit English.

## Accessibility basics
- Provide readable text size and strong contrast.
- Do not rely on color alone to indicate an important state.
- Add captions/subtitles where appropriate.
- Support control remapping where appropriate and give UI focus/navigation clear behavior.
- Test keyboard, controller, touch, and different screen sizes according to the target platform.

## Testing
Use pseudo-localization to reveal clipping early. Test every UI screen with each locale and inspect fallback behavior when an entry/asset is missing. Keep keys stable; change translations independently of code.

docs.content:
# Debugging, Testing, and Profiling

## Debugging sequence
1. Read the first Console error; later errors may be consequences.
2. Double-click it to open the source line.
3. Check filename/class name, Inspector references, active scene, and prefab instance.
4. Reproduce in the smallest scene possible.
5. Log state changes rather than every frame.
6. Remove or gate noisy logs after fixing the issue.

    Debug.Log("Reached checkpoint", this);
    Debug.LogWarning("Target has not been assigned.", this);
    Debug.LogError("Required component is missing.", this);

Passing this as context makes Console messages clickable.

## Physics debugging
- Enable Gizmos in Scene view.
- Draw casts with Debug.DrawRay or Debug.DrawLine.
- Verify layer masks, collider sizes/offsets, body type, constraints, and collision matrix.
- Check trigger callback Rigidbody requirements.
- Check whether the collider is on a child while the script checks only the root.

## Profiler
Open Window → Analysis → Profiler. Profile a Development Build on target hardware when possible; Editor overhead changes results. Measure CPU, GPU, memory, garbage collection, rendering, and physics separately.

## Frequent failures
NullReferenceException: missing reference, destroyed object, or initialization-order issue. Missing script: class/file mismatch or deleted/renamed class. Input not detected: wrong map/backend/binding or focus. Physics jitter: Transform writes conflict with Rigidbody simulation. Build-only failure: missing scene, case mismatch, platform API, unsupported package, or Editor-only code.

docs.content:
# 2D Tilemaps, Sprite Import, and Collision

## Sprite import
Set Texture Type to Sprite (2D and UI). Use Single for one sprite or Multiple for a sheet. Slice multiple sprites in Sprite Editor. Pixels Per Unit determines how many source pixels correspond to one world unit. Filtering and compression depend on art style and target; pixel art commonly uses Point filtering and careful camera/PPU alignment.

## Tilemap workflow
1. Create a 2D Tilemap, usually Rectangular.
2. Create a Tile Palette and drag sprites in to create Tile assets.
3. Separate decorative tiles from solid collision tiles when practical.
4. Add TilemapCollider2D to the collision Tilemap.
5. For large maps, consider CompositeCollider2D to merge adjacent tile boundaries. Configure the TilemapCollider2D composite operation and Rigidbody2D setup according to the installed Unity version.
6. Set the collision Tilemap's layer and verify the Physics 2D collision matrix.

## Collision best practices
- Use composite geometry where it reduces seams and collider overhead.
- Inspect collider outlines in Scene view.
- Check Tile asset Collider Type and TilemapRenderer sorting settings.
- Ensure player Rigidbody2D and collider match the movement controller.
- Keep collision and decorative layers separate if their behavior differs.

## Common problems
- Player falls through: missing/disabled collider, layer matrix, or incompatible body setup.
- Player catches on seams: try a composite collider and tune collider geometry.
- Wrong render order: configure Sorting Layer and Order in Layer.
- Blurry pixel art: check filter mode, PPU, camera scaling, and pixel-perfect setup.

## Guides
- [Input System setup](./Input-System-Setup.md)
- [Touch and mobile input](./Touch-and-Mobile-Input.md)

## Input System workflow
Install the Input System package, create an Input Actions asset/action map, define expected value types, assign it to PlayerInput, and select a notification behavior. Send Messages uses callback names matching the actions; Unity Events uses explicit Inspector wiring.

## Design rules
Keep input collection separate from movement/gameplay. A keyboard/gamepad Vector2 or virtual joystick should produce the same intent value where possible. Capture one-shot presses such as jump, then consume them deliberately in the physics step.

## Troubleshooting
Check the active input backend, default action map, bindings, callback names/signatures, UI input module, and focus. Verify mobile touch controls with realistic device aspect ratios and touch interactions.

Official docs: https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem@latest

# 2D: Movement

Choose a movement authority and keep it consistent. Separate input collection from movement so controls can later be replaced by AI, replay, or touch input.

## Guides
- [Platformer controller](./Platformer-Controller.md)
- [Jump buffer and coyote time](./Jump-Buffer-and-Coyote-Time.md)
- [Top-down movement](./Top-Down-Movement.md)
- [Moving platforms](./Moving-Platforms.md)
- [Ground checks and LayerMasks](../Physics/Ground-Checks-and-Layer-Masks.md)

## Platformer checklist
Use horizontal acceleration/deceleration as desired, a small ground overlap/cast, jump buffering/coyote time, variable jump height, terminal fall speed, and deliberate moving-platform behavior. Keep sprite facing separate from physics velocity when appropriate.

## Top-down checklist
Read Vector2 input, normalize if diagonal movement should not be faster, and choose whether the character rotates or flips. Use a consistent physics approach.

## Physics timing
For Dynamic Rigidbody2D movement, use Rigidbody2D APIs with physics-step timing. For kinematic movement, understand MovePosition behavior and collision limitations. Avoid arbitrary Transform movement competing with Rigidbody control.

## Debugging
Draw the ground probe, verify LayerMasks and collider geometry, and log input/grounded state. Reference: [Rigidbody2D API](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Rigidbody2D.html)

docs.content:
# 2D: Optimization

Measure before optimizing. Use the Unity Profiler on a representative build and device.

## Areas to inspect
- Texture memory, sprite atlas usage, compression, and asset dimensions.
- Transparent overdraw from large overlapping sprites and effects.
- Frequent instantiate/destroy patterns for projectiles, enemies, and particles.
- Physics query frequency, collider complexity, and layer masks.
- UI rebuilds, allocations, and unnecessary per-frame work.

## Practical approach
Record a baseline, identify the bottleneck, change one thing, then profile again. Object pooling and atlases can help in the right context, but neither is automatically faster for every project. Test builds rather than relying solely on Editor performance.

Reference: [Unity Profiler](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/Profiler.html)

docs.content:
# 2D Joints and Rope Mechanics

Joints connect Rigidbody2D objects with constraints. Use joints when you want the physics solver to manage a connection instead of manually moving both objects.

## Common joint components
- DistanceJoint2D: keeps connected anchors a target distance apart; useful for rope-like links.
- SpringJoint2D: allows spring-like motion with distance/frequency/damping behavior.
- HingeJoint2D: allows relative rotation around an anchor, useful for swinging objects.
- FixedJoint2D: constrains connected objects to a fixed relative pose.
- SliderJoint2D: constrains motion along one axis.
- WheelJoint2D: suspension/wheel-like motion with spring behavior.
- RelativeJoint2D: constrains relative motion with configurable offsets.
- TargetJoint2D: pulls a Rigidbody2D toward a target position.

Exact fields differ by joint and Unity version. Consult each component's Inspector tooltips.

## Distance joint setup
1. Create two GameObjects with Rigidbody2D and Collider2D.
2. Add DistanceJoint2D to one body.
3. Assign Connected Rigidbody or leave it unset for a world connection, depending on the intended behavior.
4. Configure anchor/connected anchor, Auto Configure Connected Anchor, distance, and collision between connected bodies.
5. Test with the body's mass and gravity settings; anchors need to align with the desired attachment points.

## Rope made from linked segments
For a rope/chain, create multiple small bodies with Collider2D and Rigidbody2D, connect adjacent segments with DistanceJoint2D or HingeJoint2D, and use sensible mass/collider sizes. Too many segments increase solver work and jitter risk. Enable collision between linked bodies only if self-collision is necessary.

## Troubleshooting
- Joint pulls toward the wrong point: inspect anchor spaces and Auto Configure Connected Anchor.
- Chain jitters: shorten chain, tune masses, limit collision complexity, and inspect solver settings.
- Object spins unexpectedly: inspect anchor positions and Rigidbody constraints.
- Joint does nothing: body reference missing, component disabled, or connected body setup incorrect.

Official reference: https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/Joints2D.html

# 2D One-Way Platforms

A one-way platform should allow the player to land from above while letting them pass through from below. Unity's Platform Effector 2D is usually the easiest built-in approach.

## Inspector setup
1. Put the platform on a Ground layer.
2. Add a BoxCollider2D and enable Used By Effector (label may vary slightly by Unity version).
3. Add PlatformEffector2D to the same GameObject.
4. Configure Surface Arc and Use One Way as appropriate.
5. Ensure the player's Rigidbody2D/Collider2D setup interacts with the platform and test from above and below.

Effector settings and collider compatibility matter; use the installed Inspector tooltips for the exact version. Do not add a second solid collider that blocks the player from below.

## Drop down
A game may temporarily ignore a one-way platform collider while the player presses down+jump. Use a reference to the specific platform collider and re-enable it after a short timer. Do not disable every platform globally, and ensure the player's feet don't remain inside the collider when it re-enables.

## Common mistakes
- Collider is not configured to be used by the effector.
- A second collider still blocks the player from below.
- Platform is on a layer excluded by the player's collision matrix.
- Drop-through code never re-enables the collider.
- The player re-enables collision while still overlapping the platform and gets pushed/stuck.

docs.title: 2D Physics Materials, Friction, and Bounciness
docs.content:
# 2D Physics Materials, Friction, and Bounciness

Physics Material 2D controls friction and bounciness on Collider2D components. It is different from a rendering Material. Create it through Assets → Create → 2D → Physics Material 2D, then assign it to a Collider2D's Material field.

## Friction
High friction resists sliding during contact. Low friction lets objects slide more easily. If the player stops abruptly when input ends, friction may contribute, but movement code also matters; a controller that writes velocity directly can override friction's expected effect.

## Bounciness
Bounciness controls how much collision velocity is retained on impact. A bounce may feel different with different masses, velocities, contact geometry, and combine settings. For predictable gameplay bounce pads, consider explicitly setting the player's vertical velocity when activated instead of relying entirely on material bounce.

## Combine behavior
When two colliders touch, Unity combines material values based on the configured friction/bounce combine modes. Labels and available options may vary by Unity version. Inspect both colliders when results seem unexpected.

## Troubleshooting
- Player slides: inspect material friction, Rigidbody2D damping, and movement code.
- Object barely bounces: inspect bounciness, combine modes, mass, and incoming speed.
- Collisions feel different on tile edges: inspect collider geometry and consider a CompositeCollider2D.
- The material changes surface appearance only: a rendering Material was assigned instead of Physics Material 2D.

Official API: https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/PhysicsMaterial2D.html

# 2D: Physics

## Guides
- [Queries and collision matrix](./Queries-and-Collision-Matrix.md)
- [Physics2D query reference](./Physics2D-Query-Reference.md)
- [Ground checks and LayerMasks](./Ground-Checks-and-Layer-Masks.md)
- [One-way platforms](./One-Way-Platforms.md)
- [Physics materials and friction](./Physics-Materials-and-Friction.md)
- [Joints and rope mechanics](./Joints-and-Rope-Mechanics.md)
- [Projectiles and damage](./Projectile-and-Damage.md)
- [Melee/area hitboxes](./Melee-and-Area-Hitboxes.md)

## Body types
- Dynamic: participates in force/gravity simulation and collision response.
- Kinematic: controlled by code, not driven by forces in the same way as Dynamic.
- Static: represents geometry that does not move under simulation.

## Callbacks and queries
Solid contact callbacks include OnCollisionEnter2D, OnCollisionStay2D, and OnCollisionExit2D. Trigger callbacks include OnTriggerEnter2D, OnTriggerStay2D, and OnTriggerExit2D. Queries include Raycast, CircleCast, BoxCast, and overlap methods.

Physics Material 2D controls friction and bounciness. The Physics 2D Layer Collision Matrix decides which layers interact. Use LayerMasks to filter irrelevant objects.

## Troubleshooting
Confirm colliders are enabled and overlapping as expected, check trigger/Rigidbody setup, verify layer settings, and use exact callback signatures. Use physics-step timing for physics-driven movement. [Physics2D API](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Physics2D.html)

docs.content:
# Pixel-art import settings

Consistent import settings are essential for crisp tile-based and sprite-based games.

## Recommended starting point

For each pixel-art texture:

- **Texture Type:** Sprite (2D and UI)
- **Sprite Mode:** Single or Multiple for a sheet
- **Pixels Per Unit:** choose a consistent value across tiles and characters
- **Filter Mode:** Point (no filter)
- **Compression:** None for strict pixel fidelity, or test platform compression visually
- **Generate Mip Maps:** usually off for flat 2D pixel art
- **Mesh Type:** Tight or Full Rect depending on slicing and batching needs

Settings may vary by art style and target platform; verify the result in a built player as well as the Editor.

## Pixels Per Unit example

If a tile is 16 pixels wide and PPU is 16, it occupies about one world unit. A 32-pixel tile at PPU 32 also occupies one world unit. The player sprite, tilemaps, and camera should use a consistent scale.

## Sprite sheet slicing

1. Open the texture's Sprite Editor.
2. Choose Slice and select Grid by Cell Size or Cell Count.
3. Enter the actual cell dimensions.
4. Inspect each slice for padding and alignment.
5. Apply, then verify the sprites in the Project window.

## Common problems

- Blurry sprites: check filtering, compression, PPU, and camera scaling.
- Lines between tiles: inspect sprite padding, atlas settings, and subpixel camera positions.
- Different sprite sizes: standardize PPU or intentionally scale individual assets.
- Camera shimmer: use a pixel-perfect camera workflow if exact pixel alignment is a requirement.

# 2D: Rendering

## Guides
- [Sorting layers and pixel art](./Sorting-Layers-and-Pixel-Art.md)
- [Parallax background](./Parallax-Background.md)

## Sprite rendering
SpriteRenderer draws a sprite with a selected material and color. Sorting Layer provides broad order; Order in Layer orders renderers within that layer. Z depth and transparency sorting can also matter depending on the camera/project settings.

## Import and pixels
Use Sprite (2D and UI) texture type. Choose Single for one sprite or Multiple for sheets. Keep Pixels Per Unit consistent. Point filtering is common for pixel art; Bilinear may suit smooth art. Test filter/compression settings at target resolution.

## Parallax
Move distant background layers by a fraction of camera movement. Use camera delta rather than repeatedly adding absolute camera position, and keep each layer's movement owned by one script.

## Common mistakes
Wrong sorting layer/order, mismatched PPU, inconsistent pivots, fractional camera movement in pixel art, and background Z/order that covers gameplay.

docs.title: 2D Rendering: Sorting Layers, Sprite Import, and Pixel Art
docs.content:
# 2D Rendering: Sorting Layers, Sprite Import, and Pixel Art

## Sorting rules
SpriteRenderer has a Sorting Layer and Order in Layer. Sorting Layers are ordered in the Tags and Layers settings; within a layer, larger order values render in front of smaller ones. TilemapRenderer also exposes sorting controls. Do not confuse a render Sorting Layer with a GameObject physics Layer.

## Sprite import checklist
- Texture Type: Sprite (2D and UI).
- Sprite Mode: Single for one image or Multiple for a sheet.
- Pixels Per Unit: keep consistent across assets designed at the same world scale.
- Filter Mode: Point for crisp pixel art; Bilinear often suits smooth artwork.
- Compression: select based on target quality and memory constraints.
- Sprite Editor: slice the sheet and confirm pivots and borders.

## Pixel-perfect camera
For pixel art, use consistent PPU, matching art/reference-resolution choices, and the 2D Pixel Perfect package if appropriate. Test camera movement at actual target resolutions. Fractional positions/scales can create blurry or uneven pixel steps.

## Top-down Y sorting
In a top-down game, objects nearer the bottom of the screen often need to draw in front of objects farther up. Configure the SpriteRenderer's mode appropriately for the project, or assign order based on a consistent Y-sorting rule. If multiple renderers are on one character, keep their ordering coordinated.

## Transparency and render order
Transparent sprites can cover one another according to sorting settings rather than depth-writing like opaque geometry. Use the Frame Debugger and Scene view to diagnose unexpected draw order.

Common mistakes: mismatched Sorting Layer names, two scripts fighting over order, wrong pivots causing visual jumps, incorrect PPU, and physics Layer changes used to try to fix visual sorting.

# 2D: Tilemaps

## Main pieces
- **Grid:** defines cell layout and spacing.
- **Tilemap:** stores tile data for cells.
- **Tilemap Renderer:** draws the tilemap.
- **Tile Palette:** editor workflow for painting tiles.
- **Tilemap Collider 2D:** builds collision shapes from tiles.
- **Composite Collider 2D:** can combine adjacent outlines when configured with a suitable Rigidbody2D setup.
- **Rule Tiles:** can select sprites based on neighbours when the required package is installed.

Step-by-step collision setup: [Tilemap Collision Workflow](./Tilemap-Collision-Workflow.md).

## Layer design
Use separate tilemaps for ground, decoration, foreground, collision, hazards, and interactive tiles when their sorting or collision needs differ. Not every decorative tile needs a collider.

## Troubleshooting
Check the Tile Palette asset, active tilemap, sorting layer, collider enable state, and physics layer matrix. When using Composite Collider 2D, verify the Rigidbody2D and composite operation settings.

Reference: [Tilemap manual](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/Tilemap.html)

docs.title: Tilemap Collision Workflow
docs.content:
# Tilemap Collision Workflow

## Recommended hierarchy
```text
Grid
├── GroundTilemap
├── DecorationTilemap
├── CollisionTilemap
└── ForegroundTilemap
```

Use separate Tilemaps when sorting, collision, or editing responsibilities differ. Decorative tiles should not automatically receive collision.

## Setup
1. Create a Grid and Tilemap using the 2D Tilemap menu.
2. Open Window → 2D → Tile Palette and create/select a palette.
3. Add sprites as tiles and paint the map.
4. Add TilemapCollider2D to the collision tilemap only.
5. If merging adjacent shapes is useful, add a CompositeCollider2D and configure the TilemapCollider2D to contribute to it; verify the required Rigidbody2D and composite settings for your Unity version.
6. Set the collision tilemap's Layer and check Project Settings → Physics 2D.
7. Test corners, ledges, and narrow passages in Play mode.

## Collider choices
- TilemapCollider2D creates collision geometry from tiles.
- CompositeCollider2D can combine compatible shapes, reducing seams and collider count.
- Rigidbody2D is commonly configured as Static for non-moving level geometry, depending on the composite setup.

## Common issues
- Collider is on the wrong Tilemap.
- Decorative tilemap accidentally blocks the player.
- Physics layer matrix prevents contact.
- Composite setup is incomplete or not generating geometry.
- Tile sprite pivot or cell size makes visuals look misaligned.

Reference: [Tilemap Collider 2D](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-TilemapCollider2D.html)

The guides here use Unity's built-in uGUI system unless stated otherwise. uGUI uses Canvas, RectTransform, Graphic, EventSystem, and UI components.

## Guides
- [Health bar and HUD](./Health-Bar-and-HUD.md)
- [Buttons, menus, and pause](./Buttons-Menus-and-Pause.md)

## Layout basics
Use Canvas Scaler with Scale With Screen Size for scalable screen UI. Use RectTransform anchors and layout groups rather than fixing all positions to absolute pixels. Import TextMeshPro essentials if prompted.

## Input troubleshooting
Verify an active EventSystem and the input module that matches the chosen input backend. Buttons may be blocked by overlapping raycast targets, disabled CanvasGroup settings, or missing On Click listeners. A world-space Canvas has different scale and rendering concerns from a screen-space Canvas.

## Accessibility and test
Test multiple aspect ratios, support readable contrast and meaningful labels, and do not rely on color alone to communicate state.

# 3D: AI and Navigation

## Guides
- [State machines and NavMesh basics](./State-Machines-and-NavMesh.md)
- [Patrol and target detection](./Patrol-and-Detection.md)

## NavMesh workflow
Use an AI Navigation package compatible with the installed Unity version. Add/configure NavMeshSurface where required, bake navigable surfaces, and keep each NavMeshAgent on the baked mesh. Check radius, height, stopping distance, speed, acceleration, and obstacle settings.

## Behavior design
A small finite state machine commonly includes Patrol, Chase, Attack, and Return. Keep state transitions explicit. Use distance for simple awareness and a raycast for line of sight; distance alone allows enemies to detect through walls.

## Troubleshooting
- No baked/valid path or agent is off the NavMesh.
- Target or waypoint is missing.
- Two scripts control the same agent destination or Transform.
- Detection/attack range values use inconsistent world units.
- Frequent recalculation causes unnecessary work.

Import and configure the rig/Avatar, create clips, make an Animator Controller, add typed parameters, then connect states and transitions. Keep parameter names and types consistent with scripts. Use a Blend Tree for locomotion blending when it simplifies transitions.

Decide if animation-authored displacement or controller code owns movement. Avoid both independently moving the same character. Test clip interruption because animation events that close hitboxes may not run if a clip is interrupted.

## Spatial setup
Keep one active AudioListener, normally on the player camera. Set a world-space AudioSource's Spatial Blend toward 1, configure Min/Max Distance and rolloff, and place the source on the object producing the sound.

Route sources to AudioMixer groups for SFX, music, dialogue, and ambience. Expose mixer parameters for settings controls. Convert linear UI volume to decibels when controlling an exposed mixer volume parameter.

If a sound is silent, check clip/source enabled state, Play On Awake/manual Play call, listener, source and mixer volume, spatial distance/rolloff, AudioListener pause, and whether the object has been disabled/destroyed.

# 3D: Cameras

## Guides
- [First- and third-person camera foundations](./First-and-Third-Person-Camera.md)
- [Third-person camera collision and smoothing](./Camera-Collision-and-Smoothing.md)

## Key camera settings
Projection selects Perspective or Orthographic. Perspective Field of View controls the viewing angle; near/far clipping planes define visible depth. Culling Mask selects rendered layers. Check transform axes and local versus world positions when setting a camera offset.

## First person
Separate character yaw from camera pitch. Lock the cursor only during gameplay and unlock it for menus/pause.

## Third person
Use a target pivot and a desired offset behind the player. Add wall-collision handling, avoid colliding with the player itself, and integrate camera smoothing into one system. Cinemachine may be preferable for complex follow rigs and confiners.

## Common problems
- Camera clips through walls or the player.
- Mouse look rotates movement axes incorrectly.
- Cursor remains locked while settings are open.
- Camera clipping planes or culling mask hide objects.

docs.title: Common 3D Components: What to Inspect
docs.content:
# Common 3D Components: What to Inspect

This is a practical overview, not a substitute for the version-specific Manual or API.

## Transform
Position, rotation, scale, and parent/child hierarchy. Confirm world versus local space. Negative scale and non-uniform parent scale can produce confusing orientation and physics behavior.

## Rigidbody
Simulates motion and physical response. Key settings: Mass, Linear/Angular Damping, Use Gravity, Is Kinematic, Interpolate, Collision Detection, Constraints. Avoid writing Transform position every frame on a dynamic body. Unity 6 exposes linearVelocity; older APIs may use velocity.

## Collider types
- BoxCollider: boxes and simple hitboxes.
- SphereCollider: round objects and triggers.
- CapsuleCollider: characters and elongated objects.
- MeshCollider: geometry-shaped collision; dynamic use has convex limitations.
- Is Trigger: overlap events instead of solid contact response.

Tune collider center/size/radius/height independently of visible mesh where practical.

## CharacterController
A capsule-based character mover using Move or SimpleMove. Move does not automatically apply gravity; gameplay code must handle vertical velocity. Inspect Height, Radius, Center, Slope Limit, Step Offset, Skin Width, and Min Move Distance.

## Camera
Projection (Perspective/Orthographic), Field of View or Orthographic Size, Clipping Planes, Culling Mask, Depth, and pipeline properties. A small far clip or wrong culling mask can make objects disappear.

## MeshRenderer / SkinnedMeshRenderer
Materials, shadow casting/receiving, probe settings, and enabled state. SkinnedMeshRenderer also requires a valid rig and skin weights.

## Animator
Controller, Avatar, Apply Root Motion, Update Mode, Culling Mode. Parameter names/types and transition conditions must match the controller.

## AudioSource
Clip, Volume, Pitch, Loop, Play On Awake, Spatial Blend, Min/Max Distance, Output Mixer Group. Usually keep one active AudioListener on the player camera.

## Canvas / EventSystem
Canvas render mode and sorting; Canvas Scaler and anchors; EventSystem plus an input module matching the project input backend. For uGUI clicks, inspect Graphic Raycaster, Raycast Target, and CanvasGroup.

## Troubleshooting
If a component appears ineffective, verify it is enabled, its GameObject is active, references are assigned, layers/masks permit interaction, the correct physics system is used, and the Scene/Game views are not hiding the result.

docs.title: 3D Component Inspector Reference
docs.content:
# 3D Component Inspector Reference

Inspector labels and available fields vary with Unity version, package, and render pipeline. Treat this as a conceptual guide and use the Editor tooltips for the installed version.

## Rigidbody

| Property | Purpose / when to change it |
|---|---|
| Mass | Affects response to forces and collisions. |
| Drag / Linear Damping | Resists movement over time; label varies by version. |
| Angular Drag / Angular Damping | Resists rotation over time. |
| Use Gravity | Enables gravity for a Dynamic body. |
| Is Kinematic | Changes the body to code-driven physics behaviour. |
| Interpolate | Smooths rendered movement between physics updates. |
| Collision Detection | Discrete is cheaper; Continuous modes can help fast objects avoid tunnelling. |
| Constraints | Freezes position or rotation axes. |

## Collider
- **BoxCollider:** boxes, crates, walls, and simple rectangular shapes.
- **SphereCollider:** round objects and simple detection volumes.
- **CapsuleCollider:** characters and elongated rounded objects.
- **MeshCollider:** matches mesh geometry; more expensive and has restrictions for moving rigidbodies.
- **Is Trigger:** detects overlaps without ordinary solid blocking.
- **Material:** friction and bounciness.
- **Center / Size / Radius / Height:** define shape placement and dimensions.

## CharacterController
- **Slope Limit:** steepness the controller can climb.
- **Step Offset:** maximum step height the controller can step onto.
- **Skin Width:** tolerance around the capsule; too small can increase sticking/jitter.
- **Min Move Distance:** small moves below this may be ignored.
- **Center, Radius, Height:** define the capsule volume.

## MeshRenderer
- **Materials:** material slots used to render submeshes.
- **Shadow Casting / Receive Shadows:** shadow behaviour.
- **Light Probes / Reflection Probes:** indirect lighting data sources.
- **Motion Vectors / Rendering options:** pipeline-dependent rendering features.

## Camera
- **Projection:** Perspective or Orthographic.
- **Field of View:** perspective viewing angle.
- **Clipping Planes:** near and far visible distances.
- **Culling Mask:** layers rendered by the camera.
- **Viewport Rect:** portion of the screen occupied by the camera.

## Diagnostic order
Check active state, assigned references, layers, collider geometry, Rigidbody configuration, camera culling, material/shader compatibility, then Console errors.

Official references: [Rigidbody](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Rigidbody.html) · [Collider](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Collider.html) · [CharacterController](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/CharacterController.html)

docs.content:
# 3D: Components

## Common components
- **Transform:** world/local position, rotation, and scale.
- **MeshFilter + MeshRenderer:** static mesh geometry and rendering.
- **SkinnedMeshRenderer:** renders deforming meshes driven by a skeleton.
- **Rigidbody:** physics simulation, mass, drag/damping, gravity, kinematic state, interpolation, collision detection, and constraints.
- **Collider:** Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh, and Terrain colliders.
- **CharacterController:** collision-constrained movement driven by script rather than standard Dynamic Rigidbody simulation.
- **Animator:** evaluates animation states and parameters.

Detailed settings reference: [3D Component Inspector Reference](./Inspector-Reference.md).

## Selection guidance
Use simple colliders where possible. A CharacterController and a Dynamic Rigidbody are different movement architectures. Avoid putting a non-convex MeshCollider on a moving Rigidbody unless the documented setup supports it.

## Inspector troubleshooting
Check references, collider dimensions, Rigidbody settings, enabled state, layer matrix, material assignments, and camera culling. Avoid unnecessary non-uniform scaling on physics hierarchies.

Reference: [Component API](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Component.html)

docs.title: Common Unity APIs: Quick Reference
docs.content:
# Common Unity APIs: Quick Reference

## GameObject and components

    GetComponent<Rigidbody>()
    GetComponentInChildren<Collider>()
    TryGetComponent(out Rigidbody body)
    gameObject.SetActive(false)
    GetComponent<Renderer>().enabled = false

Cache references in Awake when used repeatedly. GetComponent searches the requested object; use parent/child lookup when hierarchy placement requires it. Avoid scene-wide searches in Update.

## Instantiate and Destroy

    GameObject clone = Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation);
    Destroy(clone, 2f);

Instantiate creates a runtime object. Destroy is commonly used for one-off objects; frequent effects may be better pooled. A prefab asset cannot reliably store a direct reference to an arbitrary scene instance.

## Transform

    transform.position
    transform.localPosition
    transform.rotation
    transform.localRotation
    transform.forward
    transform.right
    transform.up
    transform.TransformPoint(localPoint)
    transform.InverseTransformPoint(worldPoint)

Position is world space; localPosition is relative to the parent. TransformPoint converts a local point to world space; InverseTransformPoint does the opposite. forward/right/up represent the object's world orientation axes.

## Time and random

    Time.deltaTime
    Time.fixedDeltaTime
    Time.timeScale
    Random.Range(0f, 1f)
    Random.Range(0, count)

For integer Random.Range, the maximum is exclusive. For float Random.Range, both ends can be inclusive. Validate count before requesting a random index.

## Math and interpolation

    Mathf.Clamp(value, min, max)
    Mathf.Clamp01(value)
    Mathf.Lerp(a, b, t)
    Mathf.MoveTowards(current, target, maxDelta)
    Mathf.Approximately(a, b)
    Vector3.Distance(a, b)
    Vector3.Dot(a, b)
    Vector3.Cross(a, b)
    Vector3.Normalize(direction)
    Quaternion.LookRotation(direction)

Lerp interpolates by a fraction; repeated Lerp is not constant-speed motion. MoveTowards limits the maximum step distance.

## Scene and diagnostics

    SceneManager.LoadScene("Level01");
    Debug.Log("Message", this);
    Debug.DrawRay(origin, direction * range, Color.yellow, 1f);

Scene loading requires inclusion in the active Build Profile.

Official reference: https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/

## Coordinate spaces
Unity commonly uses X/Z for ground-plane movement and Y for vertical height, though projects may choose another convention. Transform.position is world space; localPosition is relative to the parent. Parent rotation/scale affect child world transforms.

## Geometry and rendering terms
Mesh data includes vertices, triangles, normals, and UVs. MeshFilter supplies geometry to a MeshRenderer. Material references a shader and property values. Perspective cameras apply perspective; orthographic cameras do not scale apparent size with depth.

## Common mistakes
Mixing local/world coordinates, parent-scale side effects, using Lerp for constant speed, calling LookRotation with a zero direction, and assuming ordinary properties serialize automatically.

docs.title: 3D Transforms and Essential Math
docs.content:
# 3D Transforms and Essential Math

## Position spaces
- `transform.position`: world position.
- `transform.localPosition`: position relative to parent.
- `TransformPoint`: converts a local point to world space.
- `InverseTransformPoint`: converts a world point to local space.
- `TransformDirection`: transforms a direction while ignoring position.
- `InverseTransformDirection`: converts a world direction to local direction.

A child inherits the parent's transform. If a parent rotates, the child's world position and orientation can change even if the child's local values do not.

## Vector basics
- `Vector3.magnitude`: length of a vector.
- `Vector3.sqrMagnitude`: squared length; useful when only comparing distances.
- `Vector3.normalized`: direction with length one (or zero for a zero vector).
- `Vector3.Dot(a, b)`: alignment measure; useful for front/behind and angle checks.
- `Vector3.Cross(a, b)`: perpendicular vector in 3D.
- `Vector3.Distance(a, b)`: distance between points.

## Direction and rotation
```csharp
Vector3 toTarget = target.position - transform.position;
float distance = toTarget.magnitude;

if (distance > 0.001f)
{
    Vector3 direction = toTarget / distance;
    Quaternion desiredRotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(direction, Vector3.up);
    transform.rotation = Quaternion.Slerp(
        transform.rotation, desiredRotation, turnSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
}
```

Guard against a zero direction before calling LookRotation. The example assumes the character's forward axis is Z and uses world up.

## Time
- `Time.deltaTime`: elapsed time since the previous rendered frame; use for frame-rate-independent per-frame movement.
- `Time.fixedDeltaTime`: configured physics step duration.
- `Time.time`: scaled time since play began.
- `Time.unscaledDeltaTime`: elapsed frame time unaffected by time scale.

## Common mistakes
- Comparing magnitudes when squared magnitudes are enough.
- Forgetting to multiply a per-second speed by elapsed time.
- Confusing a direction vector with a point.
- Using Euler angles for repeated incremental 3D rotation when quaternion APIs are more suitable.
- Assuming local and world values are interchangeable.

References: [Transform](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Transform.html) · [Vector3](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Vector3.html) · [Quaternion](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Quaternion.html)

docs.title: Vector Math Reference for 3D Games

# Vector Math Reference for 3D Games

## Position versus direction
A position describes a location. A direction describes an offset/orientation. Subtracting positions gives a direction:

    Vector3 direction = target.position - transform.position;
    float distance = direction.magnitude;
    Vector3 unitDirection = direction.normalized;

Use sqrMagnitude for comparisons when distance itself is not needed:

    if ((target.position - transform.position).sqrMagnitude < range * range)
    {
        // Target is within range.
    }

## Useful methods
- Vector3.Distance(a, b): distance between points.
- Vector3.Dot(a, b): alignment test; useful for checking whether a target is in front.
- Vector3.Cross(a, b): perpendicular vector.
- Vector3.ProjectOnPlane(v, normal): remove a component perpendicular to a plane.
- Vector3.MoveTowards(current, target, maxDistanceDelta): bounded step.
- Vector3.Lerp(a, b, t): interpolation between values.
- Quaternion.LookRotation(direction): face a direction.
- Quaternion.Slerp(a, b, t): interpolate rotations.
- Mathf.Clamp(value, min, max): constrain a number.
- Mathf.Atan2(y, x): angle from components, useful for 2D aiming.

## Camera-relative movement
For ground-plane movement, camera forward includes pitch. Project it onto the horizontal plane:

    Vector3 forward = Vector3.ProjectOnPlane(camera.forward, Vector3.up).normalized;
    Vector3 right = Vector3.ProjectOnPlane(camera.right, Vector3.up).normalized;
    Vector3 move = forward * input.y + right * input.x;
    move = Vector3.ClampMagnitude(move, 1f);

Clamping magnitude prevents diagonal movement from being faster than straight movement.

## Dot product and field of view
For normalized forward and target direction, dot is 1 when aligned, 0 at 90 degrees, and -1 when opposite. A threshold can make a simple cone test. Use a raycast if physical line of sight matters.

## Lerp versus MoveTowards
Lerp interpolates by a fraction; repeated small fractions approach the target asymptotically. MoveTowards moves by a bounded distance. SmoothDamp is useful for damped movement. Constant-speed movement is often better expressed with MoveTowards or velocity.

## Common mistakes
- Normalizing a vector whose magnitude is still needed.
- Adding positions where a direction was intended.
- Comparing magnitude when squared magnitude suffices.
- Passing a zero direction into LookRotation.
- Multiplying mouse delta by deltaTime without considering how the input value is defined.

# 3D Debugging and Profiling

## First-error workflow
1. Read the first Console error.
2. Open the indicated source line.
3. Check object references, active state, component dependencies, and input actions.
4. Reproduce in a minimal scene.
5. Verify build-specific and platform-specific behavior.
6. Remove temporary logs after fixing the cause.

## Physics visualization
Draw rays using Debug.DrawRay and hit points using Gizmos or debug lines. Inspect collider bounds, Rigidbody interpolation, collision mode, layers, and the collision matrix. When a CharacterController sticks, inspect capsule center/height, skin width, slope limit, step offset, and scene geometry.

## Profiler workflow
Open Window → Analysis → Profiler. Use a Development Build on target hardware for realistic results. Inspect CPU, GPU, memory, garbage collection, rendering, physics, and audio. A slow Editor frame may not reflect standalone build performance.

## Common errors
- NullReferenceException: reference is unassigned, destroyed, or not initialized in time.
- MissingReferenceException: a Unity object was destroyed but code still holds a reference.
- Physics jitter: mixed Transform and Rigidbody movement, or unsuitable interpolation/timestep.
- Mesh/material invisible: culling mask, clipping planes, renderer state, shader, or missing material.
- Animation not driving movement: Animator state/parameters/root-motion setup conflict.
- NavMeshAgent doesn't move: agent isn't on a baked NavMesh, path is invalid, or another script conflicts.
- Build fails while Editor runs: unsupported API/package, missing scene/content, or Editor-only code included in runtime.

## Profiling priorities
Measure before optimizing. Reduce allocations, expensive physics operations, excessive real-time lighting, unnecessary object churn, repeated scene-wide searches, and over-frequent AI updates only when profiling shows those systems are costly.

# 3D: Debugging and Profiling

## Guide
- [Debugging and profiling](./Debugging-and-Profiling.md)

## Workflow
Read the first Console error, open the source line, inspect scene references and component states, then reproduce with the smallest scene. Validate package/version support for build failures. Use Gizmos and Debug.DrawRay to inspect query origins and hit directions.

## Profile rather than guess
Use Window → Analysis → Profiler and test Development Builds on target hardware. Separate CPU, GPU, memory, garbage collection, physics, rendering, AI, and audio costs. Make one change at a time and profile again.

## Common diagnosis
- Null reference: missing object/reference or initialization ordering.
- No raycast hit: wrong mask, origin inside geometry, range too short, or trigger filtering.
- Rigidbody jitter: conflicting Transform writes or poor physics interpolation setup.
- NavMesh movement failure: invalid path, missing bake, or agent off mesh.
- Render problem: culling mask, clip planes, shader/pipeline mismatch, or disabled renderer.

# Game Architecture and Scene Flow

## A practical small-game structure
- Input reader translates devices into intent.
- Controller converts intent into movement.
- Health/damage owns health and death events.
- UI presenter displays state without owning gameplay rules.
- Game-flow manager handles pause, game over, and level changes.
- ScriptableObjects store shared authored definitions.
- Save system persists progress separately from scene objects.

Do not create a class for every tiny feature. Choose the simplest structure that keeps ownership clear.

## Scene flow
Use SceneManager and include scenes in the active Build Profile. If a manager uses DontDestroyOnLoad, prevent duplicates and plan cleanup. Do not let several scripts independently own global time scale, audio volume, or scene transitions.

## Dependencies
Use serialized references for scene-local dependencies. Use events for notifications. Use interfaces when different concrete object types share behavior. Global singletons can be convenient but hide dependencies and complicate tests.

    public interface IDamageable
    {
        void TakeDamage(float amount);
    }

A weapon can call TakeDamage on any object implementing IDamageable. Interfaces are ordinary C#, but serializing interface references in the Inspector requires a wrapper or a serialized Unity object reference with a cast.

## Checklist
- Every state has a clear owner.
- Event subscribers unsubscribe when disabled or destroyed.
- Scene transitions restore pause/time state.
- Authored definitions are separate from mutable save data.
- Missing references produce clear errors.
- UI is not the only place where gameplay rules exist.

## Guides

- [Saving/loading JSON](./Saving-Loading-JSON.md)

## Recommended ownership
Keep gameplay state separate from presentation. Health owns health values; game flow determines death behavior; UI reads state; inventory owns runtime item counts; ScriptableObjects hold item definitions; save data stores stable IDs/counts instead of scene object references.

## Testing checklist
Test repeated callbacks, missing references, pause/resume and scene transitions, invalid save data, full inventory stacks/overflow, and objects destroyed while prompts still refer to them.
